article.title: Weakening the Very Courts
article.author: Stephen Rohde
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Courtesy of Los Angeles Lawyer Magazine As the Supreme Court begins its new term, with some very important cases on its docket, [1] we must take a serious look at what the Court—or, more specifically, the six-member conservative supermajority of justices appointed by Republican presidents—has done thus far in President Donald J. Trump’s second term. Not only has the Roberts Court cleared the way for Trump’s aggressive agenda to be implemented, thereby vastly expanding unchecked presidential power, it has done so by enlarging its own power and displacing and degrading the role of the lower federal courts. This is the disturbing conclusion of “The Court Against the Courts,” a comprehensive and well-documented hundred-page foreword to the Harvard Law Review’s annual assessment of the Court’s most recent term, written by prominent Supreme Court scholar Stephen I. Vladeck. Vladeck, who is the Agnes Williams Sesquicentennial Professor of Federal Courts at Georgetown University Law Center, examines key decisions from the Court’s past term in detail. His analysis is cogent and well argued. It makes a significant contribution to the growing body of legal literature that is documenting in real time the significant role the Roberts Court is playing in creating an imperial presidency. Vladeck sees a Supreme Court that has supplanted district courts, “no longer sitting in review . . . so much as in their place .” [2] He argues that the Court “has done significant damage to the formal, practical, and moral authority of federal district courts to hold the federal government to account—while arrogating some of those same courts’ powers to itself.” [3] Related: The Crackdown on Pro-Palestinian Speech: How Universities Are Silencing Dissent Vladeck divides his argument into three parts, the first of which focuses on “challenges district courts have encountered” in litigating the current administration, followed by a section in which Vladeck argues that the Court is going beyond “undermining” the lower courts and is now behaving “as if it is a court of first impression.” [4] The third and final part of Vladeck’s argument is perhaps his most substantive. Here, Vladeck ties together his hundred-page foreword by demonstrating how the Court has “made it much harder for federal courts to hold the executive branch accountable” as well as how the Court’s actions “have further enabled executive branch lawlessness” and makes a plea for “restoring the authority of district courts.” [5] Before he makes his case, Vladeck hastens to note that district courts are not infallible, nor should they enjoy unbounded power to halt executive action nationwide. But even if one supports recent substantive results by the Court, Vladeck asserts, the “systematic transfer of authority away from the trial courts” should still be troubling. [6] Vladeck wisely places the Roberts Court’s belittling of lower federal courts in the context of what he calls “a sustained, multi-front assault without precedent in American history” directed at federal judges since Trump returned to office by the executive branch, administration officials, and even the United States Senate. [7] Vladeck fears that these vicious executive and legislative attacks have contributed to the significant increase in threats on judges around the country, noting that, according to the U.S. Marshals, “there were 564 threats against federal judges in fiscal year 2025, with 275 already logged in just the first three months of 2026.” The attacks are sustained and cruel, with Vladeck highlighting that early in 2025, several judges received anonymous pizza deliveries in the name of Daniel Anderl, the murdered son of Judge Esther Salas, as well as an example of one federal judge who received over 400 threatening voicemails. [8] Vladeck reports that all of this is occurring alongside “an unprecedented volume of lawsuits challenging . . . the Trump administration.” [9] Habeas petitions filed by immigration detainees are one glaring example where Vladeck highlights a dramatic increase, noting “we’ve gone from fewer than 1,000 such cases nationwide each year to more than 3,400 per month .” [10] Not only is the volume of litigation unprecedented, but “so too is the rate of executive branch defiance of federal court orders—including more than 50 documented instances in New Jersey and more than 200 in Minnesota.” [11] Vladeck reminds readers of several prominent cases where no meaningful effort was made by the Trump administration to comply with federal orders, including J.G.G. v. Trump , where a federal court barred “transfers of Venezuelan detainees to El Salvador” but “the government nevertheless allowed two planeloads to land in El Salvador.” [12] Similarly, Vladeck highlights the Trump administration’s failure to comply with the Court’s unanimous Noem v. Abrego Garcia decision, doing “nothing to ‘facilitate’ the return of a man it conceded had been wrongfully removed to CECOT.” [13] In addition to direct noncompliance, Vladeck also cites a study documenting the far broader and subtler rise of “legalistic noncompliance.” [14] Although Vladeck suggests that it would be reasonable to assume that the Supreme Court would come to the defense of the lower federal courts, this has not been the case in reality. [15] Even if the Court isn’t “affirmatively endorsing the executive and legislative efforts to undermine lower courts . . . its behavior has enabled them.” [16] A year ago, in the pages of this publication, I, too, observed how the Court was protecting Trump by casting aside lower court rulings against him. “[A]lthough scores of federal trial and appellate courts have issued hundreds of temporary restraining orders, preliminary injunctions, and final judgments intended to curb Trump’s abuse of power, the conservative majority on the U.S. Supreme Court has used its emergency docket, dubbed the ‘shadow docket,’ to create a law-free zone enabling Trump to implement executive orders—orders already found unconstitutional by lower courts—that immediately disrupt the status quo while appeals are pending.” [17] Related: UCLA 9/11 Symposium Sparks Battle Over Academic Freedom I noted that, while in 2024 the Roberts Court invented absolute presidential criminal immunity in Trump v. United States , now it was also allowing Trump to ignore “Congress and radically disrupt or dismantle important federal institutions in the face of the text and history of the Constitution and well-established Supreme Court precedents.” I recalled the admonition of George Washington that because ambitious leaders possess a “love of power and proneness to abuse it,” at its best the Court should serve as an indispensable “guardian” upholding the “necessity of reciprocal checks of political power,” and I expressed the hope that there was “still time for the Court to resume that crucial role in the American democracy.” [18] Unfortunately, as Vladeck compellingly describes, the Court hasn’t heeded such warnings. Instead, “the Court has repeatedly stayed, narrowed, or vacated district court orders blocking executive action—often without full briefing, oral argument, or reasoned explanation.” [19] Vladeck cites several recent cases where decisions were delivered via the emergency docket, but notes that the issue is not simply the method of delivery, but that “these maneuvers placed district and circuit courts in a doctrinal vise.” [20] Vladeck’s most disturbing finding is how cavalierly the Court’s majority casts aside the detailed factual records amassed in the district courts courts that often spend weeks and sometimes months evaluating extensive testimony and written evidence. He offers the glaring example of a five-paragraph ruling in December 2025 in Abbott v. League of United Latin American Citizens . There, the majority, stating only that its order was “[b]ased on our preliminary evaluation of this case,” [21] “stayed a three-judge district court’s injunction that had blocked Texas’s new congressional map.” But it gets worse. Vladeck points out that just a few months later, in April 2026, the Court reversed the lower court on the merits —solely “[f]or the reasons set forth” in its brief 2025 order, despite the fact that a three-judge federal panel conducted what Vladeck characterizes as an “unusually extensive preliminary injunction proceedings: a nine-day evidentiary hearing featuring 23 witnesses, thousands of exhibits, hours of video footage of legislators and the Governor, and a record spanning roughly 3,000 pages.” The panel issued a 160-page opinion on November 18, 2025, finding “substantial evidence that Texas racially gerrymandered the 2025 Map,” and enjoining its use in the 2026 elections.” [22] Vladeck cleverly anticipates that “a skeptical reader will almost certainly respond by pointing to how poorly President Trump fared before the Supreme Court during the October 2025 Term.” [23] And it is true that the Court has shot down certain efforts by the Trump administration, with Vladeck reminding us of the Court’s outright rejection of Trump’s tariffs and his efforts to place limits on birthright citizenship, as well as the Court’s role in stopping Trump from deploying the National Guard around Chicago. [24] Nevertheless, Vladeck argues that an emphasis on Trump’s failures before the Court “obfuscates both how those cases reached the Supreme Court and how the justices both undermined and arrogated the authority of lower courts along the way, whether intentionally or otherwise, in those cases and others.” According to Vladeck, while it may be true that “ empowering the courts won’t fully constrain a sufficiently determined executive” it’s nevertheless the case that “kneecapping them at this moment could prove especially catastrophic.” [25] Related: A Hawaii Justice Puts the Roberts Court on Trial One of the most powerful sections of Vladeck’s foreword is when he invokes one of Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson’s memorable dissents, in which Justice Jackson herself invokes Justice Robert H. Jackson’s celebrated concurrence in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer , [26] commonly referred to as the Steel Seizure Case. In a landmark decision limiting presidential authority, the Court held that President Harry S. Truman lacked the power to seize the steel mills during the Korean War in the absence of statutory authority conferred on him by Congress. With all its defects, delays and inconveniences, men have discovered no technique for long preserving free government except that the Executive be under the law, and that the law be made by parliamentary deliberations. Such institutions may be destined to pass away. But it is the duty of the Court to be last, not first, to give them up. [27] Vladeck observes that the current Justice Jackson “was insisting that the responsibility to keep the executive ‘under the law’ . . . falls on the whole federal judiciary, not just the Supreme Court.” A “holistic assessment” of what has happened over the past eighteen months suggests that both Justices Jackson were, in Vladeck’s view, “close to the mark.” [28] Less than a month after returning to the White House, President Trump embraced the imperial decree attributed to French Emperor Napoleon Bonaparte: “He who saves his Country does not violate any Law.” [29] Only a few months later, seeing how Trump was already acting egregiously above the law, Celina Stewart, CEO, and Dianna Wynn, president, of the League of Women Voters, declared that “our country is in a constitutional crisis.” They decried how the “foundational principles that have sustained our democracy — checks and balances, the rule of law, free and fair elections — are under direct and sustained threat.” Calling it an “extraordinary moment,” in which “we cannot proceed with business as usual,” they implored all Americans, regardless of whom they had voted for in 2024, “to come together, stand united, and fight back to save our democracy. We cannot afford to fail the generations to come.” [30] In this dark period in American history, marked by a supine and groveling Congress and an irrational and power-hungry President, it is illuminating—cautionary—to see an outstanding legal scholar like Vladeck squarely place a considerable share of the blame for our constitutional crisis on the third branch of our government for its corrosive role in the deterioration of our essential constitutional institutions. Diagnosing the disease that has infected the Supreme Court is the first step to curing it, and to healing the American body politic.
